{{Puzzles}}  
In [[geometry]], a '''tetrad''' is a set of four [[simply connected]] disjoint planar regions in the plane, each pair sharing a finite portion of common boundary. It was named by Michael R. W. Buckley in 1975 in the ''[[Journal of Recreational Mathematics]]''. A further question was proposed that became a puzzle, whether the 4 regions could be congruent, with or without ''holes'', other enclosed regions.<ref name=gardner>Martin Gardner, ''Penrose Tiles to Trapdoor ciphers'', 1989, p.121-123 [https://books.google.com/books?id=P1AFEAAAQBAJ&dq=Michael+R.+W.+Buckley+tetrad&pg=PA121]</ref>

== Fewest sides and vertices==
The solutions with four congruent tiles include some with five sides.<ref name=trump>[https://www.trump.de/tetrads/ Further Questions about Tetrads] by Walter Trump </ref> However, their placement surrounds an uncovered hole in the plane. Among solutions without holes, the ones with the fewest possible sides are given by a hexagon identified by Scott Kim as a student at Stanford University.<ref name=gardner/> It is not known whether five-sided solutions without holes are possible.<ref name=trump/>
:[[File:Hexagonal tetrad.svg|240px]]

Kim's solution has 16 vertices, while some of the pentagon solutions have as few as 11 vertices. It is not known whether fewer vertices are possible.<ref name=trump/>

== Congruent polyform solutions==
Gardner offered a number of [[polyform]] ([[polyomino]], [[polyiamond]], and [[polyhex (mathematics)|polyhex]]) solutions, with no holes.<ref name=gardner/>
<gallery>
Tetrad-solution6.svg|11 squares
Tetrad_solution3.svg|12 squares
Tetrad_solution2.svg|10 triangles
Tetrad_solution5.svg|22 triangles
Tetrad_solution4.svg|26 triangles
Tetrad_solution1.svg|4 hexagons
</gallery>
